result.output:
# Changelog

All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/),
and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/).

## [Unreleased]

### Fixed

- **`BootstrapLogger` now receives the bootstrap planning and progress lines.** They went only to the `-v` stderr log, so an embedder saw the GitHub size lookup and then nothing until the first checkpoint upload. A bootstrap that stalled while planning logged the size preflight and then nothing until its timeout. Every planning line now also goes to `BootstrapLogger`, with the logger's own attributes and the caller's context. Phase and checkpoint progress goes at Info: planning checkpoints, fetching the commit graph, planned remaining branches with their counts, push attempting, group pushed, branch finalized. A push the target refused or timed out, and resume markers left on the target, go at Warn; a push git-sync stops itself at its byte budget and then splits stays at Info, so a successful bootstrap logs no warnings. Lines logged once per branch (subsumed by trunk, already on target) go at Debug, so a repository with thousands of branches does not emit thousands of Info records per attempt. Error text from the target is sanitized. `-v` shows every line it showed before. ([#134](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/134))
- **Batched bootstrap of a repository with thousands of branches now makes progress.** It used to fetch the commit graph of every branch, one request per branch, before it pushed anything. On a branch-heavy repository that planning alone outlasted a 30-minute sync budget, so each attempt timed out with nothing on the target and started again (ENT-3617). The trunk is now planned and pushed first, so an attempt that times out still leaves it on the target. The remaining branches share one commit-graph fetch. Small branches are pushed in shared packs that create their refs directly, so a fetch and a push deliver many of them. A group whose pack is over budget splits in half. A branch too big to share a pack, or one with a resume marker, keeps its own checkpointed batch as before. `FetchCommitParents` now takes the wants as a list of hashes.
- **Replicate no longer gets stuck after an interrupted bootstrap.** Replicate routes to batched bootstrap only when every desired ref is missing on the target. A bootstrap cut short after the trunk landed left the next run on plain replicate, which sends every missing branch in one pack; a target with a request body limit refused it, and every retry sent the same pack again. When the target refuses replicate's pack for its size or a push deadline, replicate now creates the missing refs with batched bootstrap, planned in one commit-graph fetch against the refs the target already has, then pushes the remaining updates and deletes. Such a run reports relay reason `replicate-pack-rejected`.
- **SSH sources now negotiate protocol v2.** git-sync sent `GIT_PROTOCOL` as a prefix of the remote command, which hosts without a login shell reject (GitHub answers "Invalid command"), so `auto` fell back to v1 on every SSH sync and re-read the full ref advertisement on each RPC. It now sets `GIT_PROTOCOL` in the ssh environment and passes `-o SendEnv=GIT_PROTOCOL`, as git does. A server that does not accept the variable answers v0/v1 and `auto` falls back as before; `--protocol v2` against such a server fails with "source did not negotiate protocol v2". This includes servers that run a login shell but whose sshd does not list `GIT_PROTOCOL` in `AcceptEnv` (stock OpenSSH accepts only `LANG LC_*`): they used to reach v2 through the command prefix and now get v1, as they do with git itself, until `AcceptEnv GIT_PROTOCOL` is added.
- SSH fetches from GitHub intermittently failed with `update object storage: empty packfile`. The SSH transport wrote the request and closed stdin while the server was still streaming its ref advertisement (36 MB for `NixOS/nixpkgs`), and GitHub sometimes dropped a request that arrived that early. The request is now sent only after the advertisement is read, which is what `git` does. On the old code, 2 of 4 runs against `git@github.com:NixOS/nixpkgs.git` failed; with the change, 7 of 7 passed.
- Errors from closing an upload-pack stream (the ssh exit status and the remote's stderr) were dropped in `fetchToStoreV1` and `fetchToStoreV2`, because `CheckClose` wrote to a shadowed `err`. They are now joined into the returned error.

## [0.10.0] - 2026-10-21

### Security

- Bumped the Go toolchain to `1.27.3` (go.mod `toolchain` and the mise pin), clearing GO-2026-6809: `crypto/x509` now distrusts compromised intermediate certificates. It is reachable through TLS verification on every HTTPS remote. ([#126](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/126))

- Bumped the Go toolchain to `1.27.2` (go.mod `toolchain` and the mise pin), clearing ten standard-library advisories reachable from the HTTP transport and the `convert-sha256` filesystem paths — among them HTTP/1 client desynchronization after a `CONNECT` rejection (GO-2026-6605), a memory-limit bypass parsing MIME headers in `net/textproto` (GO-2026-6608), malformed ECH outer extension references accepted by `crypto/tls` (GO-2026-6607), and HTTP/2 transport accepting malformed framing headers (GO-2026-6610). I've moved go-git and go-billy to `v6.0.0-beta.1` and updated the other dependencies. Go itself can't be updated: 1.27.3 is already the latest release, so the toolchain pin is unchanged. The code builds, `go test -race ./...` passes, and golangci-lint reports 0 issues. I didn't run govulncheck because it isn't installed here. Nothing is committed.

**Dependency bumps:**
- **Direct:** go-git and go-billy alpha → `beta.1`, testify `1.11.1` → `1.12.1`.
- **Indirect:** x/net `0.62.0`, x/sync `0.24.0`, ProtonMail/go-crypto `1.5.2`, circl `1.6.5`, sha1cd `0.7.0`, go-winio `0.6.4`, pflag `1.0.10`.
- **Cleanup:** `go mod tidy` removed a few indirect entries that are no longer needed.

**One behavior change from go-git beta.1.** `TestPartitionRefNamesRejectsDangerousNames/leading_dash_on_a_branch` failed after the bump. go-git's ref-name check now accepts names that start with a dash, like `refs/heads/-oProxyCommand=id`. Upstream made this change on purpose to match git, which only blocks a leading dash when you create a branch or tag; `git fetch` and `git clone` copy such refs without complaint.

I followed upstream instead of adding our own dash check, for two reasons:
- **It's what the code says it should do.** The comment in `internal/gitproto/refnames.go` says git-sync uses go-git's check so that "nothing git considers legitimate is skipped".
- **No command-injection path.** The only place a ref name reaches a command line is the `git tag -s converted/<name> refs/heads/<name>` call in `sha256convert`, and neither of those arguments can start with `-`.

So refs like `refs/heads/-foo` are now mirrored instead of skipped. I updated the doc comment and moved that test case into the "keeps legitimate names" test. If you'd rather keep rejecting these names as extra hardening, it's a two-line check in `PartitionRefNames`.

I also added a "Changed" entry under Unreleased in `CHANGELOG.md` covering the bumps and the leading-dash change.

Stefan Haubold Wed Aug 19 15:14:37 2026 +0200

Validate ref names arriving from a remote

Nothing checked the names a remote advertises, and git-sync acts on them
in two ways that make a malformed one dangerous.

convert-sha256 writes them to disk. go-git resolves a ref name through
the repository filesystem, so "refs/heads/../../config" escapes
refs/heads. go-billy clamps the traversal at the repository root, so this
is repository corruption rather than arbitrary file write — but config,
HEAD, and packed-refs are all in range, with the content constrained to
an object hash.

Ref-update commands embed them in the receive-pack request. receive-pack
reads a feature list from everything after the first NUL on a command
line, so a source advertising a name containing NUL can inject
capabilities into the push git-sync sends to the target.

Validation defers to plumbing.ReferenceName.Validate, which implements
git's check_refname_format: "..", NUL, CR, LF, other control characters,
DEL, space, "~^:?*[", backslash, "@{", a ".lock" suffix, a leading dot,
empty components, and a leading dash on a branch or tag. Deferring rather
than hand-rolling keeps git-sync's notion of a valid ref identical to
git's, so nothing git considers legitimate gets skipped — verified
against refs/pull/*, refs/notes/*, and nested branch names.

It runs at the two decode boundaries (AdvRefsToSlice and decodeV2LSRefs)
rather than at each call site, so every path that reads an advertisement
is covered by construction, on both the source and target side. A skipped
target ref is also one the planner never sees, so it is never picked as a
prune candidate — the safe direction.

Bad names are skipped with a warning rather than failing the run,
matching how per-ref push rejections behave under BestEffort: one
malformed ref upstream should not stop a mirror. The warning prints names
with %q, because they are remote-controlled and an embedded escape
sequence would otherwise reach the terminal; the individual list is
capped while the count still covers everything skipped.

--map values get the same validation but are rejected outright rather
than skipped. They are configuration, and a mapped target ref reaches the
same places an advertised one does, so failing at startup beats silently
not mirroring what was asked for.

We never decided to reject them. The rejection came along with go-git's validator, which happened to include that rule at the time.

The rule was added in 0f6a015e ("Validate ref names arriving from a remote"). That commit was written against two specific threats:

1. **Path traversal in `convert-sha256`.** A name like `refs/heads/../../config` gets written through the repository filesystem and can overwrite `config`, `HEAD` or `packed-refs`.
2. **Capability injection into receive-pack.** A name containing NUL lets the source slip extra capabilities into the push git-sync sends to the target.

Neither threat involves a leading dash. To defend against them, the commit used go-git's `ReferenceName.Validate` instead of writing its own check, so that git-sync's idea of a valid ref would match git's. In alpha.5, `Validate` also rejected a leading dash on branches and tags, so the commit listed it among the rules it was picking up.

That list was slightly wrong. It describes the whole set as git's `check_refname_format`, but git doesn't apply the dash rule there. It applies it only when you create a branch or tag (`check_branch_ref` / `check_tag_ref`). go-git beta.1 fixed exactly that mismatch.

The test case's label, "argument-injection shape", reads like a reason. But it describes what the name looks like, not a path in git-sync where it could be exploited. As I checked earlier, no ref name lands in an argument position where git would read it as an option.

Dropping the rejection is in line with what the commit was trying to do: match git, block traversal and NUL, and skip nothing git accepts. There's one more effect to know about. `--map` values go through the same `Validate` call in `internal/validation/validation.go:219`, so a mapping like `refs/heads/-foo` is now accepted at startup instead of rejected. That's consistent with the rest, and no test covered it either way.
